Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 32
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 5
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 23
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 5
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

The application is setting the server port. To migrate a Java application that sets the server port to Azure Container Apps:

Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that has reached its End of OSS Support.
With the officially supported new versions from Spring, you can get the best experience. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose a supported Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and determine the most suitable supported Spring Boot version.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Upgrading to a supported version ensures better performance, security, and compatibility with modern tools.
1. Pick a Supported Version: Review the Spring Framework support policy and choose an actively supported version.
2. Update Your Project: Change the Spring Framework version in your pom.xml or build.gradle.
3. Fix Compatibility Issues: Update deprecated code, replace removed features, and ensure dependencies are compatible with the new Spring Framework version.
4. Thoroughly Test: Run unit, integration, and end-to-end tests to make sure everything still works after the upgrade.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is one deployable application with server-rendered pages, a multipart upload contract, and database-backed image delivery. These diagrams describe checked-in implementation and configuration, not verified running infrastructure.

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle holds both photo metadata and image bytes in one table; uploads do not write image files to disk. Legacy filename/path fields and one bundled static image remain for compatibility. Local Compose provides a persistent database volume, while the test profile selects H2. No application cache, message broker, or outbound business API client was found. Browser assets depend on jsDelivr. The separate Azure setup script provisions AKS, ACR, and PostgreSQL 15, but there is no corresponding PostgreSQL driver or runtime profile in the application; those resources are not represented as active application dependencies.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Constructor injection connects controllers to a shared transactional service and one repository; there are no independently deployable domain microservices.
  • The same database record owns metadata and BLOB content; the gallery query also selects BLOBs. Native Oracle queries create a database-specific persistence boundary.
  • Reads are public; upload/delete require authentication. No application-side HTTPS listener is configured, and TLS termination outside the repository cannot be established.

API & Service Communication Contracts

Five explicit controller mappings expose HTML browsing, JSON multi-file upload feedback, binary photo delivery, and deletion by redirect. All application and database interactions are synchronous; no versioned API or inter-service gateway is defined.

Service Catalog

ServicePortCategoryPurpose
photo-album / Compose photoalbum-java-app8080BusinessOne source-built module; Spring MVC/Thymeleaf, Spring Security, Spring Data JPA
Compose oracle-db1521InfrastructureThird-party Oracle Free container; not a source-built application module

The Azure resource provisioning script is not evidence of a deployed application service or an additional runtime API.

API Endpoints Inventory

ServiceMethodPathRequest TypeResponse Type
Photo Album / HomeControllerGET/No typed request200 HTML index model; database failures produce an empty-gallery model
Photo Album / HomeControllerPOST/uploadmultipart/form-data, repeated required files parts bound to List200 JSON Map with success, uploadedPhotos, failedUploads; empty supplied collection returns 400 with success=false and error; missing required binding normally yields framework 400
Photo Album / DetailControllerGET/detail/{id}String path ID200 HTML detail; absent/invalid ID or load failure redirects to / (normally 302)
Photo Album / DetailControllerPOST/detail/{id}/deleteString path ID; no body modelRedirect to / (normally 302) with success/error flash attribute
Photo Album / PhotoFileControllerGET/photo/{id}String path ID; browser may append an ignored cache-busting query200 ResponseEntity using stored MIME type; 404 for absent record or empty bytes; 500 for caught serving errors

Upload results can mix successes and failures in one 200 response. Even when every file fails business checks, the normal controller result is 200 with success=false, not a per-file HTTP error. Multipart transport limits are framework-level constraints; no custom exception-to-status mapping is defined. Both POST mappings require authentication; unauthenticated requests receive the Basic authentication challenge/401.

No Actuator dependency is declared. Framework fallback error handling is not an explicitly authored business endpoint.

DTOs & Contracts

  • Photo is a mutable service-owned entity used in HTML models and selected upload response projections, not an exposed entity-wide JSON resource.
  • UploadResult is a mutable per-file service outcome POJO. The controller converts it into success/failure maps; it is not returned directly.
  • The upload envelope is an untyped map containing success and failure collections. There is no immutable DTO, gateway aggregation DTO, or explicit schema contract. Persistence fields are documented in data-architecture.md.
  • MVC supplies normal Jackson JSON serialization through the JSON/web starters; there is no custom serializer or explicit date-format configuration. The browser converts the returned upload timestamp using new Date(...).
  • Binary delivery uses the recorded MIME type and includes X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, and X-Photo-Size headers plus cache-prevention headers.
  • No OpenAPI document, protobuf, GraphQL schema, API version qualifier, or versioning header was found in the analyzed application files.

Communication Patterns

Browser-to-server HTTP, constructor-injected controller-to-service calls, and service-to-repository/JDBC calls are synchronous. Upload processing is sequential over files; it is not background or message-driven processing. No outbound REST client, broker, discovery client, gateway, aggregation across services, client-side load balancer, retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback service, or explicit network/request timeout is defined in application configuration.

Error degradation is local: gallery database errors render an empty gallery; detail lookup/errors redirect; image errors return 404/500; upload business failures appear in per-file results. There is no automatic replay or downstream retry. Database readiness gates local application startup; see configuration-inventory.md for the exact mechanism.

SecurityConfig configures stateless HTTP Basic with a BCrypt-encoded in-memory administrator. Upload and delete require an authenticated caller; the configured account has an ADMIN role, but endpoint rules use authentication rather than role/ownership checks. Reads and other unmatched requests are permitted. CSRF is disabled. No application-side TLS listener is configured; local Compose exposes HTTP. External TLS termination and deployed identity policies cannot be inferred from these files.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Local environment interpolation requires ORACLE_PASSWORD, APP_USER_PASSWORD, and APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD before Compose can create services; missing required values fail early.
  2. Oracle starts with its data volume and initialization scripts. Its health check executes the image's healthcheck.sh every 30 seconds, with a 10-second timeout, 15 retries, and a 180-second start period.
  3. Photo Album waits for Oracle via Compose depends_on: condition: service_healthy, then constructs the datasource, ORM context, and administrator bean. Oracle readiness does not prove all app-specific queries or credentials work.
  4. oracle-init/create-user.sh contains a fixed 30-second delay; this is distinct from the Compose health check. The separate healthcheck.sql is not the command referenced by Compose.
  5. No application health check/readiness probe, explicit application startup timeout, or config/discovery-server chain is defined.
  6. The Azure script sequentially provisions resources and waits 30 seconds before database user setup; it does not start the application or establish runtime readiness.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

Local operation expects a user-created dotenv file based on .env.example. Compose interpolates required secret variables, passes Oracle administrative/schema credentials to the database container, and binds schema and administrator credentials into the application environment. Spring resolves datasource settings and the administrator bean; the administrator password is encoded with BCrypt for the in-memory user store. There is no detected encrypted-at-rest dotenv format, Jasypt layer, Vault/Key Vault integration, or managed identity for database access.

Oracle scripts create/grant the schema user using injected settings, though some grant/verification SQL assumes a fixed schema identifier; changing APP_USER alone does not update those SQL statements. The Azure setup script uses an existing Azure CLI login, accepts or generates PostgreSQL passwords, creates database access, and writes output settings to a git-ignored dotenv location. AKS is attached to ACR for image pull access; this is not application database secret delivery. The provisioning script and Compose use the same dotenv filename for different settings, so execution would need deliberate configuration coordination. No script was executed during this assessment.

Core Business Workflows

Users browse a shared photo gallery, open individual images, and move between older/newer uploads. Authenticated administrators can upload multiple files and delete photos; there are no user-owned albums, sharing invitations, or approval workflows.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhoto Album / photo collectionAn uploaded image and the information needed to display and navigate itStandalone aggregate; no album, owner, or user entity
UploadResultPhoto Album / upload handlingTransient success/failure outcome for one submitted fileRefers to a newly accepted photo or identifies the rejected file; not persisted

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
PhotoServiceImpl in the single Photo Album deploymentPhoto intake, gallery reading, navigation and removalPhoto; constructs UploadResultRepository/database and local image-header reader
Browser gallery/upload clientUser interaction; not an independently deployed backendNo authoritative domain statePhoto Album HTTP contracts and CDN presentation assets

This is one bounded context, not a multi-service domain. The service/repository is authoritative; newly rendered browser cards are only a projection of accepted photos.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Submit Multiple Photos

  1. A visitor selects/drops files. The browser applies the Client upload allowlist and size rules and shows local failures; accepted candidates proceed together.
  2. Submission enters POST /upload. The security filter requires authentication before controller processing.
  3. The controller checks for a provided file collection, then calls the service sequentially for each file.
  4. The service applies Server MIME allowlist, Nonempty bounded upload, and Image pixel budget rules. It generates compatibility naming and attempts to inspect dimensions without fully decoding the image.
  5. Accepted files become new photos with generated identities and upload times. Each service call persists metadata and content within its own transaction.
  6. The controller reads each successful photo back to construct the response projection and collects failures separately.
  7. The browser prepends successful photos to the gallery and displays rejected-file messages. Mixed outcomes are retained; successful uploads are not compensated because a different file failed.

There is no request-wide atomic batch, queue, deferred image processing, automatic retry, or deduplication stage.

Workflow 2: Browse the Gallery and Navigate Photos

  1. A public gallery visit loads all photos in newest-first order and renders their information.
  2. Database errors are logged and degraded to an empty gallery, which can look like an empty collection rather than an outage.
  3. Opening GET /detail/{id} loads the photo and queries both older and newer candidates. The service chooses the first result in each direction.
  4. Missing photos or detail-loading failures redirect to the gallery. At collection boundaries, unavailable navigation links are omitted.
  5. The browser separately requests the image bytes. Missing/empty content produces not-found; other caught serving errors produce a server-error response. No placeholder image fallback is implemented in the controller.

Workflow 3: Delete a Photo

  1. The detail page asks the user for a browser confirmation, then submits POST /detail/{id}/delete; authentication is required.
  2. The service looks up the photo. If absent, it reports false; otherwise it deletes the database record including its content.
  3. The controller redirects to the gallery with a success, not-found, or failure flash message.
  4. Deletion is permanent at the application level: no recycle bin, soft delete, retention timer, or compensating restore is implemented.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There is no gateway composition, distributed saga, domain event exchange, or separate photo-storage service. Browser requests, controller/service delegation, and database operations form one synchronous path. Upload responses combine per-file outcomes within one application, not responses from downstream business services.

The application joins nothing across services: image content and display information belong to the same photo record. When database access fails, local error behavior varies by entry point as described above; there is no circuit-breaker or alternate service fallback.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

RuleImplemented decision
Client upload allowlist and sizeBrowser accepts declared MIME image/jpeg, image/png, image/gif, image/webp, with an independent hard-coded maximum of 10 MiB per file
Server MIME allowlistService compares lowercased submitted content type to configured values; unsupported types fail. This is a declared-MIME check, not guaranteed signature validation
Nonempty bounded uploadService rejects files larger than configured 10 MiB or of zero/nonpositive length; multipart transport separately limits individual/request payloads
Image pixel budgetWhen ImageIO finds a reader, header width times height must not exceed 40,000,000 pixels; rejection occurs before full image decode
Optional dimensionsNo matching reader permits storage without dimensions. I/O failures cause upload failure; other caught dimension-extraction exceptions can permit continuation without dimensions
Collection requiredEmpty supplied file collection is rejected; missing required multipart binding is handled by the web framework
Maximum files settingA value of 10 is declared, but no controller/service/browser count-enforcement logic was found
Entity validationOriginal/stored filenames: nonblank, maximum 255; compatibility path maximum 500; file size non-null and positive; MIME nonblank, maximum 50; upload time non-null
Identity and namingEntity identity is a UUID; stored filename is another UUID plus original extension. Names are not deduplicated, and no uniqueness rule is enforced for original filenames
Temporal navigationOlder/newer use strict timestamp comparisons; equal-timestamp records are not adjacent candidates under these rules
Request successOverall upload success means at least one successful photo was added to the response list, not that every input succeeded
LifecycleAccepted photo becomes available for gallery reading; deletion removes it. There is no explicit domain status/state machine

Entity validation is declared with Bean Validation annotations; no controller @Valid binding is used for these programmatically created photos. JPA validation can occur during persistence, so annotated entity validation and explicit service checks are different stages.

Transactions: the service's default transaction covers each write operation; read methods are marked read-only. The controller is not transactional across the batch. Persistence exceptions caught inside the service do not guarantee recovery from a rollback-only or commit-time error.

Error handling: service upload failures carry user-oriented messages; gallery read errors render empty results; detail errors redirect; image delivery returns status errors; deletion sets flash feedback. No custom domain exception hierarchy, dead-letter queue, compensation, or retry policy was found.

Audit/logging: upload and deletion successes, file identities, and failures are logged; image delivery additionally logs metadata and a byte prefix. There is no durable business audit entity, actor-linked change history, or event stream.

Authorization: reads are public and state changes require authentication. Although the in-memory account is assigned an ADMIN role, there is no explicit role predicate, per-photo ownership, tenant boundary, or authorization inside domain service methods.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The Spring Boot 2.7.18 and Java 8 baseline predates current major Spring generations; an upgrade crosses the Java baseline and Java EE-to-Jakarta compatibility boundary. Oracle ojdbc8 is explicitly the runtime driver artifact, so changing databases requires more than a connection URL. Commons IO is explicitly pinned to 2.11.0 rather than left to central management. This is a compatibility inventory, not an advisory scan or a claim about specific CVEs; commercial support entitlements and resolved transitive versions were not assessed.

Notable Observations

  • org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-parent:2.7.18 is the sole declared parent. There are no explicit BOM imports, Maven modules, profiles, or lockfiles in this build.
  • org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-maven-plugin is the only explicitly declared build plugin; its version is inherited. Target/source Java 8 and UTF-8 encoding are explicit.
  • JSON is separately declared despite overlap with the web starter's usual dependency tree. The POM comment calls it image processing, but the declared artifact is the JSON starter, not a dedicated image-processing package.
  • No resolved transitive graph is checked in. Framework-provided logging, pooling, ORM, serialization, and test libraries must not be counted as separately declared dependencies.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

One JPA entity stores photo metadata and binary image content in Oracle; H2 is selected for the test profile. A single repository combines standard CRUD with six Oracle-native queries.

No connection pool size or pool timeout is explicitly configured. The JPA starter normally supplies framework-managed pooling, but no resolved pool version was inspected. Oracle initialization scripts grant schema privileges and verify the user; they do not provide a versioned photo-table migration or domain seed data. The bundled static image is not a database seed routine. Recreating schema can discard existing photos despite persistence of the underlying Oracle volume. There are no foreign keys, bidirectional mappings, cascades, owner/user relationships, optimistic-lock version fields, soft-delete fields, or explicit timezone policy. Validation constraints are inventoried once in business-workflows.md.

PhotoServiceImpl has class-level @Transactional; its four retrieval/navigation methods explicitly use readOnly=true. Upload/delete receive separate service-call transactions. A multi-file controller request does not have one transaction spanning every photo; post-upload lookup is another read-only service call.

Key Repository Methods

Repository: PhotoRepository extends JpaRepository, source /home/runner/work/PhotoAlbum-Java/PhotoAlbum-Java/src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java. Standard findById, save, and delete are inherited and used by the service.

All six custom methods use parameterized native SQL. Oracle-specific functions, row numbering, and column definitions limit portability to H2 or PostgreSQL; the H2 profile does not establish production-query compatibility.

Caching Strategy

No Spring Cache annotations, Redis/EhCache/Caffeine/JCache dependency or configuration, explicit cache regions/TTL, or configured Hibernate second-level/query cache was found. Hibernate's normal transaction persistence context is not a shared application cache.

Binary responses deliberately prohibit browser/proxy storage with no-cache/no-store/private headers; browser JavaScript also adds cache-busting timestamps. Gallery rendering still queries complete records, including BLOBs; there is no separate thumbnail or metadata projection cache.

Data Ownership Boundaries

One application owns one Oracle schema/table; there is no database-per-microservice topology, shared domain database access by other source-built services, cross-service join, or gateway aggregation. Reads and writes use the same entity/repository, not CQRS. Multiple app instances, if introduced, would share database records rather than a filesystem upload directory.

Photo metadata and content are persisted together. No object-store integration, audit history, retention/expiry policy, or soft-delete workflow is defined. The infrastructure script's PostgreSQL resources are a separate, unwired configuration path, not proof of replicated or migrated photo data.
